extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of early‑modern philosophy (readers of Locke)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted from John Locke's Essay concerning human understanding: a close account of how the mind forms ideas of eternity, duration, expansion (space), number, and infinity, with numbered claims and illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eternity
rubrics_metrics.description: We form the idea of Eternity by reflecting on succession and duration in our own ideas (caused by internal train of ideas or external objects) and by adding lengths of duration in thought without bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: applying the length of the sun’s annual motion to durations before the sun existed; thinking one can add such lengths in infinitum gives the notion of eternity, analogous to infinity of number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Our measures of Duration dependent on our ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Notions like hour, day, year are ideas of the length of certain periodical motions (often only present in memory) and can be applied mentally to durations antecedent to all motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The measuring of any duration by some motion does not require real co‑existence of that thing with that motion—only a clear idea of the length of a known periodical motion is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Duration of anything need not be co-existent with the motion we measure it by
rubrics_metrics.description: One can imagine different total ages of the world (e.g., 5639 years vs 50,000) with equal facility; measuring by time does not require real co‑existence with the chosen periodic motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: people of different cultures compute different world ages; one can conceive any assigned number of years by applying familiar time‑measures in thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity in Duration
rubrics_metrics.description: By repeatedly adding imagined measures of duration (minutes, hours, years) the mind can proceed in infinitum; our idea of eternity arises from this unending addibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: imagining durations before the sun by supposing the sun moved then at the same rate and counting diurnal revolutions; ties the idea of infinite duration to the infinity of number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of our ideas of duration: (First) Succession from reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: First: observing how ideas in the mind follow one another (train of ideas) yields the idea of SUCCESSION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an internal source (reflection) rather than sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of our ideas of duration: (Second) Duration from distance in succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Second: by observing a distance in the parts of succession we get the idea of DURATION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes succession (order) from duration (length between parts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of our ideas of duration: (Third) Measures from sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Third: sensation, by observing regular periodical appearances, gives ideas of certain lengths or MEASURES OF DURATION (minutes, hours, days, years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodical natural phenomena imprint standard lengths used for measuring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of our ideas of duration: (Fourth) Imagined duration without real endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourth: by repeating those measures of time in our minds we can imagine duration where nothing really endures or exists (we can imagine to‑morrow, next year, or years hence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mental repetition allows imagining durations antecedent to or independent of physical motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of our ideas of duration: (Fifth) Eternity by endless addition
rubrics_metrics.description: Fifth: by repeatedly adding ideas of any length (minute, year, age) without end we form the idea of ETERNITY as endless future duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogizes this to the endless addibility of number; both contribute to the idea of infinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of our ideas of duration: (Sixth) Time from parts of infinite duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Sixth: by considering any part of infinite duration set out by periodical measures we derive the idea of TIME in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time = determinate portions of duration distinguished by landmarks (periodical measures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Both capable of greater and less (Expansion and Duration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both expansion (space) and duration (time) are ideas of continued lengths capable of greater or less quantities; one has equally clear ideas of an hour/day as of an inch/foot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison of quantitative character: both admit magnitude increases and decreases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion not bounded by Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind can repeat an idea of any length of expansion and add it in thought, proceeding beyond all bodily extension; expansion (space) is conceivably without end even beyond bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes pure expansion (space) from extension (solid parts of matter); one can reach the end of solid extension but not of pure expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nor Duration bounded by Motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarly, duration can be enlarged in the mind beyond the existence of bodies and their motions; duration is conceivably boundless though God fills eternity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues against tying duration strictly to corporeal motions; duration can be considered antecedent to all bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why Men more easily admit infinite Duration than infinite Expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: People more readily ascribe infinity to duration (often attributed to God) than to space because duration is commonly attributed to God while extension is attributed to matter (which seems finite), leading to doubt about expansion without matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linguistic and theological habits (names and attributes) influence what people readily conceive as infinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time to Duration is as Place to Expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Time (a determinate portion of duration) relates to duration as place (a determinate portion of expansion) relates to expansion; both are landmarks within boundless oceans of duration and expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time and place are used to position finite beings relative to infinite duration/expansion; they are portions set off by known points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and Place: first acceptation (measured by existence and motion of bodies)
rubrics_metrics.description: First acceptation: time commonly is so much of infinite duration as is measured by and co‑existent with the existence and motions of the great bodies of the universe; place likewise can mean the portion of infinite space possessed by the material world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this sense, time begins and ends with the sensible world; forms phrases like 'before all time' or 'when time shall be no more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and Place: second acceptation (portions we design by measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Second acceptation: time (and place) can be applied more loosely to portions of infinite duration/space that we on occasion suppose equal to certain measured lengths (e.g., saying an event occurred at the beginning of the Julian period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We sometimes speak of times/places beyond actual measurable motions by equating them to assumed measures (e.g., saying the creation was so many Julian years ago).

rubrics_metrics.name: Where and When belong to finite beings
rubrics_metrics.description: 'WHERE' and 'WHEN' are questions applicable to finite existences and are reckoned from known parts of the sensible world and epochs marked by observable motions; without such fixed points order would be lost in infinite duration/expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions and durations of finite beings are always measured relative to sensible landmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: All the Parts of Extension are Extension, and all the Parts of Duration are Duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Although extension and duration are simple ideas, none of their distinct ideas lacks composition: both consist of parts, and every part of extension is extension, every part of duration is duration; minds use familiar measures as unit ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smallest measurable parts (in practice) serve as units (inches, minutes) though mind cannot frame indivisible pure space or time beyond these practical limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Their Parts inseparable
rubrics_metrics.description: Though parts of bodies (used to measure expansion) and parts of motion (used to measure duration) may be interrupted, the parts of expansion and duration themselves are not separable even in thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises the intimate relation between spatial and temporal parts despite interruptions like rest or sleep in their measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration is as a Line, Expansion as a Solid
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration is like a one‑dimensional line (a single straight length incapable of multiplicity or figure), while expansion (space) has breadth and thickness and can form figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains differences in how we conceive time vs. space; every present moment is common to all things (temporal unity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration has never two Parts together, Expansion altogether
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration (and time as a part of it) is perishing distance whose parts do not exist together but in succession; expansion is lasting distance whose parts exist together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to distinction: one cannot conceive two temporal parts co‑existing, whereas spatial parts co‑exist; also used to contrast finite minds' perception with God's infinite view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number the simplest and most universal Idea
rubrics_metrics.description: UNITY or one is the simplest, most universal idea; it accompanies every object, idea, or thought and thus number applies to everything that exists or can be imagined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes number as fundamental cognitive tool across domains (men, angels, actions, thoughts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Its Modes made by Addition
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex ideas of number arise by repeating the idea of unity and adding repetitions (one + one = two, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counting is the mental addition and naming of repeated units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each Mode distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple modes of number are highly distinct: any smallest variation by one unit makes a clearly different number (two distinct from one, etc.), more distinct than comparable small differences in extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This precision explains why numerical demonstrations are especially exact and applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Therefore Demonstrations in Numbers the most precise
rubrics_metrics.description: Because numerical modes are so distinguishable, demonstrations in numbers are more precise and determinate in application than demonstrations about extension, where small differences are harder to detect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 91 distinct from 90 as clearly as 91 from 9000, whereas in space one cannot as readily detect minute differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names necessary to Numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting depends on names (or marks) to represent aggregated units; without names for larger values one cannot form clear ideas or reckon those numbers reliably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language limits numerical imagination—cultures without words for large numbers cannot conceive them distinctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Another reason for the necessity of names to numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: A sparse numeral language (e.g., some American tribes without words beyond 5) prevents distinct ideas of larger numbers; distinct names for groupings (millions, billions, etc.) aid reckoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative long number formatted by group names shows difficulty of comprehension without systematic denominations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why Children number not earlier
rubrics_metrics.description: Children fail to number early either for lack of names for numerical progressions or lack of cognitive faculty to collect scattered ideas into ordered complexes and retain them in memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To count to N requires (1) distinguishing successive ideas differing by one unit, and (2) retaining the ordered series of names/marks; failure in either disrupts numeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number measures all Measurables
rubrics_metrics.description: Number is the measure the mind uses for all measurable things, chiefly expansion and duration; our idea of infinity as applied to them derives from the endless addibility of number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inexhaustible capacity to add units furnishes the clearest idea of infinity for duration and space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity attributed to Space, Duration, and Number
rubrics_metrics.description: INFINITY is primarily attributed by the mind to those things with parts (space, duration, number) capable of endless addition or subtraction; when we call God's attributes infinite we mostly conceive that infinity with respect to his duration and ubiquity, and figuratively to other inexhaustible attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautions that human ideas of divine infinity are limited and mostly analogical to numerical or extensive infinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Idea of Finite easily got
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of the finite comes readily from obvious portions of extension and ordinary periods of succession (hours, days); the problem is how the mind forms the idea of boundlessness (infinity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finite is grounded in sensory experience; infinite must be formed by mental operations beyond immediate sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: How we come by the Idea of Infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: We form the idea of infinity by recognizing that any given length of space or time (a foot, a mile, a day) can be repeated (added) in thought without ever reaching a necessary end; the power of continuing additions gives the idea of infinite space or duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: doubling an idea in thought repeatedly leaves us no nearer an end; the mind therefore abstracts an idea of endless addibility.
